notes.text: I'm going to start by calling get_mission to pull up the task details.

I'm working out a plan for six unknowns, and I'm thinking test drops could reveal the impact point, fall time, whether the drop lands in smoke, and the wind at aircraft altitude. Each drop gives wind at its own altitude, and the displacement reflects the wind integrated over the fall. I'm also weighing drops at high and low altitude to see how the wind changes with height.

I'm going to test with a drop inside the smoke column at 100 m altitude, heading 0 and speed 60, to see whether the updraft lengthens the fall. Varying the altitude across drops should also give me the wind profile.

The wind at 100 m is about 10.7 m/s from 206°, which should push the load northeast... wait, let me redo that: the displacement works out to dx=-24.7 and dy=+18.7 from the release point. The aircraft keeps flying north at 60 m/s, so over the 7.2 s fall it covers about 432 m, and the load leaves with that same forward motion.

I'm checking whether the load's forward motion really gets cancelled: with drag this strong, the load's velocity quickly matches the air's, and then the horizontal drift is mostly set by the wind rather than the aircraft's 60 m/s.

I'm working out the wind's contribution over the 7.2 s fall: it would push the load about -34 m in x and -69 m in y. But the observed displacement is only dx -24.7 and dy +18.7, so the load's horizontal velocity must have dropped to match the air almost immediately, leaving the wind to do the rest of the work.

I'm checking the rough numbers: if the load's sideways speed drops from 60 m/s to around 10, drag should carry it only about 36 m north before the wind takes over. That means the observed 18.7 m northward drift still doesn't fully line up, so I'll need to fit the drag coefficient against the data.
